mainTopic: The חורבן story: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי's meeting with אספסיינוס and his requests, and the wickedness and punishment of טיטוס
overview: This amud continues the story of the חורבן. רבן יוחנן בן זכאי proves from פסוקים that אספסיינוס will become king, and he blames the בריוני for keeping the people from making peace. אספסיינוס answers with a משל of a snake wrapped around a barrel of honey, and later sages say what רבן יוחנן בן זכאי should have answered. News comes from רומי that אספסיינוס has been made emperor. Before he leaves, he grants רבן יוחנן בן זכאי three requests: יבנה and its sages, the family of רבן גמליאל, and doctors for רבי צדוק. The גמרא then turns to the wicked טיטוס, who defiles the קדשי הקדשים and carries off the vessels of the בית המקדש, while חז"ל praise God for staying silent. When טיטוס mocks God at sea, a tiny gnat enters his brain and torments him until he dies. The amud ends with his nephew אונקלוס raising him from the dead to ask about the Jewish people, and the story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Proof from the verses that אספסיינוס will be king
steps.stepSummary: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי defends calling אספסיינוס a king. ירושלים can only fall to a king, as the פסוקים show: 'אדיר' means a king, and 'לבנון' means the בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: In truth, you are a king. If you were not a king, ירושלים would not be handed over to you, as the פסוק says: 'And the לבנון shall fall by a mighty one.' 'Mighty one' only means a king, as it says: 'And their mighty one shall be of themselves.' And 'לבנון' only means the בית המקדש, as it says: 'That good mountain and the לבנון.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי answers the first complaint of אספסיינוס, who was upset at being called a king when he was not one. He proves from פסוקים that he will become king.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument chains two definitions together. 'אדיר' (mighty one) means a king, and 'לבנון' means the בית המקדש. So the פסוק 'the לבנון shall fall by a mighty one' means the בית המקדש will only fall to a king, and since אספסיינוס is about to conquer it, he must be one.

keyTerms.meaning: Mighty one, which here means a king
Lebanon, which here means the בית המקדש

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows רבן יוחנן בן זכאי using דרשה of פסוקים to read history. It also sets up the later news that אספסיינוס really does become emperor.

phrases.english: In truth, you are a king;
for if you were not a king,
Jerusalem would not be handed over into your hand,
as it is written: "And the Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one" –
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 10:34

phrases.english: and "mighty one" means only a king,
as it is written: "And their mighty one shall be of themselves, etc.";
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 30:21. The rest of the פסוק calls this person a ruler, which shows 'mighty one' means a king.

phrases.english: and "Lebanon" means only the Temple,
as it is stated: "That good mountain and the Lebanon."
phrases.notes: דברים 3:25

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the first of two complaints אספסיינוס raised just before this section.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: You will be king, because the פסוק says the בית המקדש (לבנון) falls only to a king (אדיר).

steps.title: Why he did not come out sooner: the zealots stopped us
steps.stepSummary: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי answers the second complaint. The בריוני inside the city would not let them come out to the general.
steps.simpleTranslation: And as for what you said, 'If I am a king, why didn't you come to me until now?' The zealots among us did not let us.
steps.whatsHappening: Now רבן יוחנן בן זכאי answers the second complaint: 'If I am a king, why did you wait until now to come?' His answer is that the בריוני blocked them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The general's question suggests that the Jews were his enemies by choice. רבן יוחנן בן זכאי shifts the blame onto the violent rebels inside the city. This also sets up the general's next reply, which is about those very rebels.

keyTerms.meaning: And as for what you said
They let us (here: did not let us)

phrases.english: And as for what you said: If I am a king,

phrases.aramaic: אַמַּאי לָא קָאָתֵית לְגַבַּאי עַד הָאִידָּנָא –
phrases.english: why didn't you come to me until now –
the zealots that are among us did not let us.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Second half of the same reply; answers the general's second complaint.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The בריוני inside ירושלים prevented us from coming out to you.

steps.title: The general's parable of the honey barrel and the snake
steps.stepSummary: אספסיינוס replies with a משל. If a snake is wrapped around a barrel of honey, you break the barrel to get rid of the snake. So too he must destroy the city to get rid of the zealots.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: If there is a barrel of honey and a snake is wrapped around it, wouldn't people break the barrel to get rid of the snake?
steps.whatsHappening: אספסיינוס pushes back with a משל. He is hinting that because of the zealots, he must destroy all of ירושלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The honey barrel stands for ירושלים and the בית המקדש, and the snake stands for the בריוני. The general takes רבן יוחנן בן זכאי's own excuse, the zealots, and turns it into a reason to destroy the whole city.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִילּוּ חָבִית שֶׁל דְּבַשׁ
phrases.english: He said to him: If there were a barrel of honey
and a snake wrapped around it,

phrases.aramaic: לֹא הָיוּ שׁוֹבְרִין אֶת הֶחָבִית בִּשְׁבִיל דְּרָקוֹן?
phrases.english: wouldn't they break the barrel because of the snake?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִילּוּ חָבִית שֶׁל דְּבַשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the excuse about the zealots into a reason to destroy the city.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי's hope to save ירושלים despite the zealots
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If dangerous people are inside, you destroy the container to get rid of them, so the city must fall.

steps.title: His silence, and the answer he should have given
steps.stepSummary: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי stays silent. רב יוסף (or רבי עקיבא) applies a פסוק about God confusing the wise, and says he should have answered: take tongs, remove the snake and kill it, and leave the barrel whole.
steps.simpleTranslation: He was silent. רב יוסף, and some say רבי עקיבא, read this פסוק about him: 'He turns wise men backward and makes their knowledge foolish.' He should have said to him: We take tongs, pick up the snake and kill it, and we leave the barrel alone.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי does not answer the general. A later sage steps in to show the answer that would have defeated the משל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The better reply keeps the same משל but shows it does not lead to breaking the barrel. You can remove the snake with tongs and leave the honey safe, which means killing the rebels and sparing the city. The פסוק explains why even a great חכם missed this: God made his wisdom fail at that moment.

keyTerms.meaning: He read (applied) this verse about him

steps.confusionAlert: The tongs answer was not said in the story. It is what later sages say רבן יוחנן בן זכאי should have answered.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches that the destruction was decreed from Heaven: even the wisest leader was kept from finding the answer that might have saved the city.

phrases.english: He was silent.

phrases.aramaic: קָרֵי עֲלֵיהּ רַב יוֹסֵף, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא:
phrases.english: Rav Yosef, and some say Rabbi Akiva, read about him:
"Who turns wise men backward and makes their knowledge foolish,"
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 44:25

phrases.english: he should have said to him:
We take tongs
and we take the snake and kill it,
and the barrel we leave alone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows how the general's משל could have been answered.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the conclusion of the barrel משל, not the משל itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Breaking the barrel is not the only way; the snake can be removed with tongs and the barrel kept whole.

steps.title: News from Rome and the shoe that won't go on
steps.stepSummary: A messenger arrives: the emperor has died, and the Roman nobles want to make אספסיינוס the head. He is wearing one shoe. The other will not go on, and the first will not come off, so he asks what is happening.
steps.simpleTranslation: Meanwhile a messenger came to him from Rome and said: Get up, for the emperor has died, and the important men of Rome have decided to seat you at the head. He was wearing one shoe. He tried to put on the other one, and it would not go on. He tried to take off the first one, and it would not come off. He said: What is this?
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves to a new scene: news arrives that confirms רבן יוחנן בן זכאי's prediction that אספסיינוס will be king. A strange problem with his shoe leads him to ask a question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The prediction from step 1 comes true right away, which builds the general's respect for the sage. The stuck shoe sets up the next move, where רבן יוחנן בן זכאי explains it with a פסוק.

phrases.english: Meanwhile, a messenger came to him from Rome,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: קוּם, דְּמִית לֵיהּ קֵיסָר,
phrases.english: and said to him: Rise, for the emperor has died,

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמְרִי הָנְהוּ חֲשִׁיבֵי דְּרוֹמִי לְאוֹתֹיבָךָ בְּרֵישָׁא.
phrases.english: and those noblemen of Rome say to seat you at the head.
He was wearing one of his shoes.
phrases.notes: Some versions say just 'shoe' (round brackets); the corrected wording in square brackets says 'his shoe.'

phrases.english: He tried to put on the other one; it would not go on.
He tried to pull off the first one; it would not come off.
He said: What is this?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New scene; the news confirms the prediction made in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why his shoe will neither go on nor come off.

steps.title: Good news has made your bones fat
steps.stepSummary: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי explains that the good news made his body swell, using the פסוק 'good tidings make the bone fat.'
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Do not be upset. Good news has come to you, as it is written: 'Good tidings make the bone fat.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי answers the question about the shoe. He says joy from the good news made the general's foot swell.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק teaches that good news has a real physical effect on the body. That is why the shoe no longer fits.

phrases.english: He said to him: Do not be distressed,
good news has come to you,
as it is written: "Good tidings make the bone fat."
phrases.notes: משלי 15:30

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the general's question 'what is this?'
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The good news made your body swell, as the פסוק says.

steps.title: The cure: see someone you dislike
steps.stepSummary: Asked for a cure, רבן יוחנן בן זכאי says to have someone the general dislikes pass before him, based on 'a broken spirit dries the bones.' He does this and the shoe goes on.
steps.simpleTranslation: But what is the remedy? Let a person you are displeased with come and pass before you, as it is written: 'A broken spirit dries the bones.' He did so, and the shoe went on.
steps.whatsHappening: אספסיינוס asks how to fix the problem, and רבן יוחנן בן זכאי gives a cure taken from another פסוק. It works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the reverse of the last step. Good news swells the bones, and an upsetting sight shrinks them back. Seeing someone he dislikes upsets the general, and his foot returns to its normal size.

keyTerms.meaning: You are not at ease with him (you dislike him)
It went in (the shoe went on)

phrases.english: But what is its remedy?
phrases.notes: This is אספסיינוס asking; the next line is רבן יוחנן בן זכאי's answer.

phrases.aramaic: לֵיתֵי אִינִישׁ דְּלָא מְיַתְּבָא דַּעְתָּךְ מִינֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: Let a person come with whom you are displeased,
and let him pass before you,
as it is written: "A broken spirit dries the bones."
phrases.notes: משלי 17:22

phrases.english: He did so, and it went on.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows the explanation with a practical cure based on the opposite פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Have someone you dislike pass before you, because sadness dries the bones.

steps.title: Why didn't you come sooner? We each already answered
steps.stepSummary: Impressed, אספסיינוס asks again why such wise men did not come earlier. רבן יוחנן בן זכאי says he already answered (the zealots), and the general says he too already answered (the barrel).
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Since you are so wise, why didn't you come to me until now? He said to him: Didn't I already tell you? He said to him: I also told you!
steps.whatsHappening: The general repeats his earlier question, and the two men close the argument. Each points back to what he already said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי's answer was the בריוני (step 2). The general's reply was the barrel משל (step 3), meaning the zealots are exactly why the city must fall. The exchange ends with the general's position still standing, which sets up what רבן יוחנן בן זכאי will ask for next.
steps.whatToRemember: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי's prediction from the פסוקים came true, and his wisdom about the shoe impressed the general. But the general's barrel argument was never answered, so the destruction of ירושלים still stands.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וּמֵאַחַר דְּחָכְמִיתוּ כּוּלֵּי הַאי,
phrases.english: He said to him: And since you are so wise,

phrases.aramaic: עַד הָאִידָּנָא אַמַּאי לָא אָתֵיתוּ לְגַבַּאי?
phrases.english: why didn't you come to me until now?
He said to him: But didn't I tell you?!

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אֲנָא נָמֵי אֲמַרִי לָךְ!
phrases.english: He said to him: I also told you!
phrases.notes: He means his barrel-and-snake answer: the zealots are the very reason the city must be broken.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: וּמֵאַחַר דְּחָכְמִיתוּ כּוּלֵּי הַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the earlier argument (steps 2-3) after the shoe episode.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Each side stands by his earlier answer: the zealots kept us in, and the zealots are why the city must fall.

steps.title: The general offers a gift before leaving
steps.stepSummary: אספסיינוס says he is leaving and will send someone else to continue the war, and invites רבן יוחנן בן זכאי to ask for something.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I am going away, and I will send someone else. But ask me for something that I can give you.
steps.whatsHappening: Now that he has been made ruler, אספסיינוס is leaving, and he asks רבן יוחנן בן זכאי what he wants. This sets up the famous request in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Right after the shoe episode, the general respects רבן יוחנן בן זכאי's wisdom, so he offers him a favor. His question opens the door for the answer that follows.

phrases.english: He said to him: I am going away,
and I will send another person in my place;

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא בָּעֵי מִינַּאי מִידֵּי דְּאֶתֵּן לָךְ.
phrases.english: but ask something of me that I can give you.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא בָּעֵי מִינַּאי מִידֵּי דְּאֶתֵּן לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the wisdom shown in steps 6-8, the general offers a reward.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does רבן יוחנן בן זכאי want to be given?

steps.title: Three requests: יבנה, רבן גמליאל's family, and doctors
steps.stepSummary: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי asks for יבנה and its sages, the family line of רבן גמליאל, and doctors to heal רבי צדוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Give me יבנה and its sages, the family of רבן גמליאל, and doctors to heal רבי צדוק.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי answers with three specific requests.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All three requests aim to keep Torah leadership alive: a place of learning (יבנה), the family that leads the people (רבן גמליאל), and a great sage (רבי צדוק). He does not ask to save ירושלים itself, which is what the next step criticizes.
steps.whatToRemember: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי asked for three things: יבנה with its sages, the family of רבן גמליאל, and doctors for רבי צדוק.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: תֵּן לִי יַבְנֶה וַחֲכָמֶיהָ,
phrases.english: He said to him: Give me Yavne and its sages,
and the family line of Rabban Gamliel,
phrases.notes: Literally a 'chain', meaning the line of leaders that comes from רבן גמליאל.

phrases.english: and doctors who will heal Rabbi Tzadok.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the general's offer.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: יבנה and its sages, the family line of רבן גמליאל, and doctors for רבי צדוק.

steps.title: Criticism: he should have asked to spare the city
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף (or רבי עקיבא) applies the פסוק about God confusing the wise: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי should have asked the general to leave the Jews alone this time.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף, and some say רבי עקיבא, applied to him the פסוק: 'Who turns wise men backward and makes their knowledge foolish.' He should have told him: leave them alone this time.
steps.whatsHappening: A later sage criticizes רבן יוחנן בן זכאי's choice. He says the request was too small.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This uses the same פסוק used in step 4, where רבן יוחנן בן זכאי also missed the best answer. Here the critic says the better request was to stop the attack on ירושלים completely.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef read about him,
and some say it was Rabbi Akiva:
"Who turns wise men backward and makes their knowledge foolish,"
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 44:25. It is the same פסוק quoted back in step 4.

phrases.english: he should have said to him:
let them go this time.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָרֵי עֲלֵיהּ רַב יוֹסֵף, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the wisdom of the request in step 10; step 12 answers the challenge.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי's choice of what to ask for.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: He asked for too little. He should have asked to save the whole city.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבן יוחנן בן זכאי's choice to ask only for יבנה, the family of רבן גמליאל, and doctors (step 10)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With the general offering a favor, the wise move would have been to ask him to spare ירושלים this time, not to settle for small requests.

steps.title: Defense: asking too much could have saved nothing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains רבן יוחנן בן זכאי's thinking: the general might refuse such a big request, and then not even a small rescue would happen.
steps.simpleTranslation: But he thought: maybe he will not do that much, and then even a small rescue will not happen.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבן יוחנן בן זכאי against the criticism in the last step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His request was a careful calculation, not a mistake. A modest request had a real chance of being granted. A huge one risked refusal and total loss.
steps.confusionAlert: This line is not part of the critic's words. It is the גמרא explaining רבן יוחנן בן זכאי's side.

phrases.english: But he held:
perhaps he will not do that much,
and then even a small rescue would not happen.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the criticism of step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining the reasoning behind the action
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He foolishly asked for too little.
steps.terutzMaskana: He asked for little on purpose, to make sure something would be saved.

steps.title: What were the doctors for רבי צדוק?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the request for doctors to heal רבי צדוק involved.
steps.simpleTranslation: The doctors to heal רבי צדוק: what was that about?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses the story to ask about the third request. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is how the healing was actually done.

phrases.aramaic: אָסְווֹתָא דְּמַסַּיִין לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי צָדוֹק – מַאי הִיא?
phrases.english: The doctors to heal Rabbi Tzadok: what is that about?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָסְווֹתָא דְּמַסַּיִין לֵיהּ לְרַבִּי צָדוֹק – מַאי הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the third request in step 10 to explain it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the doctors healed רבי צדוק.

steps.title: Step-by-step feeding to heal רבי צדוק
steps.stepSummary: The doctors fed him in stages: bran water, then water with coarse flour, then flour water, until his stomach slowly widened.
steps.simpleTranslation: The first day they gave him bran water to drink, the next day water with coarse flour, the next day flour water, until his stomach widened little by little.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by describing the gradual cure.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each day the food got a little heavier, so his weak stomach could adjust slowly. Moving too fast would have harmed him.

phrases.english: The first day they gave him water of bran to drink,
the next day, water of coarse flour with bran,
the next day, water of flour,
until his stomach widened little by little.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A gradual diet of bran water, then coarse flour water, then flour water, so his stomach slowly widened.

steps.title: טיטוס is sent, and a פסוק calls him a blasphemer
steps.stepSummary: אספסיינוס leaves and sends טיטוס. The גמרא applies a פסוק to טיטוס, calling him wicked for insulting God.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went and sent טיטוס. 'And he shall say: Where is their God, the rock in whom they trusted?' This is the wicked טיטוס, who insulted and blasphemed toward Heaven.
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves on to a new character, טיטוס, who takes over the war. The גמרא introduces him with a פסוק, setting up the story of his actions that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק describes an enemy who mocks the Jews' trust in God. The גמרא reads it as being about טיטוס, which tells us how he will act in the coming story.
steps.whatToRemember: אספסיינוס leaves, and the story turns to טיטוס, called wicked for insulting God.

phrases.english: He went and sent Titus.
"And he shall say: Where is their God,
the rock in whom they trusted?"
phrases.notes: דברים 32:37

phrases.english: This is the wicked Titus,
who insulted and blasphemed toward Heaven.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the main story after the side explanation and moves on to טיטוס.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The פסוק 'Where is their God' refers to the wicked טיטוס, who blasphemed God.

steps.title: טיטוס defiles the קדשי הקדשים and slashes the פרוכת
steps.stepSummary: טיטוס enters the קדשי הקדשים, sins on a ספר תורה, and cuts the פרוכת. Blood miraculously comes out, and he thinks he has killed God. A פסוק in תהלים is brought as the source.
steps.simpleTranslation: What did טיטוס do? He took a prostitute by the hand and went into the קדשי הקדשים. He spread out a ספר תורה and sinned on it. Then he took a sword and cut the פרוכת. A miracle happened and blood came spurting out, and he thought he had killed God. This is what the פסוק means: 'Your enemies roared inside Your meeting place; they set up their own signs as signs.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the story from step 15 and describes exactly how טיטוס insulted God inside the בית המקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 15 called טיטוס wicked for insulting God, and now the גמרא shows what that insult looked like. The blood from the פרוכת was a miracle, but טיטוס misread it as proof that he had won against God. The פסוק describes enemies taking their own 'signs' (the blood) as real signs.

keyTerms.meaning: The Holy of Holies, the most sacred room in the בית המקדש
The curtain in front of the Holy of Holies

steps.confusionAlert: 'He thought he killed himself' does not mean טיטוס thought he committed suicide. 'Himself' is a respectful way of saying 'God'. The גמרא avoids writing that טיטוס thought he killed God.

phrases.english: What did he do?
phrases.notes: 'He' is טיטוס, who was sent in at the end of the last step.

phrases.english: He took a prostitute by his hand
and entered the Holy of Holies,
and he spread out a Torah scroll
and committed a sin on it.
And he took a sword and cut the curtain,
and a miracle happened
and blood was spurting and coming out,
and he thought he had killed 'himself',
phrases.notes: 'Himself' is a polite way of saying God. The גמרא didn't want to write those words directly.

phrases.english: as it is said:
'Your enemies roared in the midst of Your meeting place;
phrases.notes: תהלים 74:4

phrases.english: they set up their own signs as signs.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the insult to God that step 15 mentioned.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: טיטוס desecrated the קדשי הקדשים and took the miraculous blood as proof he had defeated God, as תהלים 74:4 describes.

steps.title: אבא חנן: God is strong enough to stay silent
steps.stepSummary: אבא חנן reads 'מי כמוך חסין יה' as praising God's strength in holding back and staying silent while טיטוס cursed Him.
steps.simpleTranslation: אבא חנן says: The פסוק says 'Who is strong like You, God?' This means: who is as strong and tough as You? You hear the insults and curses of that wicked man, and You stay silent.
steps.whatsHappening: אבא חנן reacts to טיטוס's behavior by reading a פסוק about God's strength in a new way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually 'strong' sounds like strength in fighting. אבא חנן reads it as strength in self-control: God can hear terrible insults and still hold back. This answers the obvious question of why God did not punish טיטוס right away.

keyTerms.meaning: Hard, tough (here: able to hold back)
His blasphemy, his curses against God

phrases.english: Abba Chanan says:
'Who is strong like You, O God?'
phrases.notes: תהלים 89:9

phrases.english: Who is like You, strong and tough,
since You hear the insults and the blasphemy
of that wicked man, and You stay silent.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to טיטוס's blasphemy in step 16 by explaining God's silence.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God's strength shows in His holding back while טיטוס blasphemed Him.

steps.title: School of רבי ישמעאל: Who is like You among the silent
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ישמעאל makes the same point with a wordplay: read 'באלים' (among the mighty) as 'באלמים' (among the mute).
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי ישמעאל taught: The פסוק says 'Who is like You among the mighty, ה׳?' Read it as: 'Who is like You among the mute?' God stays silent like someone who cannot speak.
steps.whatsHappening: A second teaching makes the same point as אבא חנן, this time through a play on the sound of a word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word באלים sounds almost like באלמים. With that small shift, a פסוק from שירת הים becomes praise of God for keeping quiet in the face of insults. It supports אבא חנן's idea from another פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: The school (study hall) of רבי ישמעאל taught
Mute people, those who cannot speak

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught:
'Who is like You among the mighty, ה׳?'
phrases.notes: שמות 15:11

phrases.english: Who is like You among the mute.
phrases.notes: This is a play on sound: באלים is read as if it said באלמים.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Makes the same point as step 17 from a different פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God is praised as 'among the mute' because He stays silent before blasphemers.

steps.title: טיטוס ships the vessels of the בית המקדש home to boast
steps.stepSummary: טיטוס makes the פרוכת into a large basket, fills it with the Temple vessels, and loads it on a ship so he can be praised at home. The גמרא rereads a פסוק in קהלת to describe this.
steps.simpleTranslation: What else did טיטוס do? He took the פרוכת and made it into a kind of big basket. He brought all the vessels of the בית המקדש, put them in it, and loaded them onto a ship to go and be praised in his city. As the פסוק says: 'And so I saw the wicked buried, and they came, and from the holy place they would go, and they were forgotten in the city where they had done so.' Don't read 'buried' (קבורים) but 'gathered' (קבוצים). Don't read 'forgotten' (וישתכחו) but 'praised' (וישתבחו).
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues with טיטוס's next act, and the גמרא changes how two words of a פסוק are read so that it describes him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With two small letter changes, the פסוק now describes wicked people who gather things from a holy place and are praised in their city for it. That is exactly what טיטוס planned with the stolen vessels. The 'אל תיקרי' method does not erase the plain meaning of the פסוק. It adds a second layer of meaning.

keyTerms.meaning: Don't read it as ... but rather as ... (a way of rereading a word in a פסוק)

steps.confusionAlert: 'אל תיקרי' does not mean the text of the פסוק is being changed. The written פסוק stays the same; the גמרא is drawing an extra lesson from a similar-sounding word.

phrases.english: What did he do?
He took the curtain
and made it into a kind of large basket,
and brought all the vessels that were in the Temple
and put them in it,
and placed them on a ship
to go and be praised in his city,
as it is said:
'And so I saw the wicked buried, and they came,
phrases.notes: קהלת 8:10

phrases.english: and from the holy place they would go,
and they were forgotten in the city where they had done so.'
Do not read 'buried' but 'gathered';
do not read 'and they were forgotten' but 'and they were praised'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the story of טיטוס after the side comments about God's silence.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: טיטוס gathered the Temple vessels to boast at home, as קהלת 8:10 hints when read as 'gathered' and 'praised'.

steps.title: Second view: 'buried' means truly buried things
steps.stepSummary: Others keep the word 'קבורים' as written: even hidden, buried items of the בית המקדש were revealed to טיטוס's men.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: 'buried' means really buried. Even things that were hidden away were revealed to them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second way to read the same פסוק, without changing the word 'buried'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first view changed 'קבורים' to 'קבוצים'. This view keeps the plain word and explains it: the Romans found even the vessels that had been hidden or buried. So both views agree that the פסוק describes the looting; they differ only on how to read that one word.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say (introduces a second version)

steps.whatToRemember: In this section, טיטוס insults God in the קדשי הקדשים, חז"ל praise God's strength in staying silent, and טיטוס carries off the Temple vessels. קהלת 8:10 is read two ways: as 'gathered' things, or as truly 'buried' things that were uncovered.

phrases.english: There are those who say,
'buried' means truly buried,
because even things that were hidden away
were revealed to them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different reading of the word 'קבורים' from step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'קבורים' is read literally: even buried Temple items were uncovered by טיטוס's men.

steps.title: טיטוס mocks God at sea, and a heavenly voice answers
steps.stepSummary: A wave threatens to drown טיטוס. He claims the God of Israel is only strong in water, as with פרעה and סיסרא, and dares Him to fight on land. A בת קול calls him wicked and says God will send a gnat.
steps.simpleTranslation: A sea wave rose up to drown him. He said: 'It seems to me that the God of these people has power only in water. פרעה came, and He drowned him in water. סיסרא came, and He drowned him in water. Now He is rising against me to drown me in water. If He is truly mighty, let Him come up on dry land and fight me!' A בת קול came out and said to him: 'Wicked one, son of a wicked one, grandson of עשו the wicked! I have a lowly creature in My world, and its name is the gnat.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story of טיטוס goes on: on his way home by ship he is caught in a storm and mocks God. A בת קול answers his challenge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: טיטוס reads history wrongly. He thinks God's past punishments (פרעה, סיסרא) show that His strength is limited to water. The בת קול accepts his 'dare' to fight on land, and will do it with the weakest creature possible, to show that God's power has no limit.

keyTerms.meaning: A big sea wave or storm surge

phrases.english: A wave of the sea rose against him to drown him.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: כִּמְדוּמֶּה אֲנִי שֶׁאֱלֹהֵיהֶם שֶׁל אֵלּוּ,
phrases.english: He said: It seems to me that the God of these people
has power only in water.
Pharaoh came, and He drowned him in water;
Sisera came, and He drowned him in water;
phrases.notes: See שופטים 5:21, where the river קישון sweeps away סיסרא's army.

phrases.aramaic: אַף הוּא עוֹמֵד עָלַי לְטוֹבְעֵנִי בַּמַּיִם.
phrases.english: He too is rising against me to drown me in water.
If He is mighty, let Him come up onto dry land
and make war with me!
A heavenly voice came out and said to him:
Wicked one, son of a wicked one,
grandson of Esau the wicked,
I have a lowly creature in My world,
and its name is the gnat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story of טיטוס, who had loaded the Temple vessels on a ship (step 19). Now he is at sea.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: טיטוס mocks God's power as limited to water, and a בת קול declares that God will fight him with a tiny gnat.

steps.title: Why is the gnat called a lowly creature?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא stops the story to ask why the בת קול called the gnat a 'בריה קלה.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Why is it called a 'lowly creature'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא briefly steps out of the story to ask about one phrase. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every creature is small compared to God, so the גמרא wants to know what makes the gnat especially 'lowly.' It is asking for the meaning of the word, not challenging the story.

phrases.english: Why does it call it a 'lowly creature'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the phrase 'בריה קלה' that the בת קול used in step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What makes the gnat a 'lowly' creature.

steps.title: The gnat has a way in but no way out
steps.stepSummary: The gnat is called lowly because it has an opening for taking in food but no opening for letting waste out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it has an entrance, but it does not have an exit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its question: the gnat is 'lowly' because its body is incomplete, with an opening to eat but none to get rid of waste.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that the gnat is one of the most incomplete and weak creatures there is. That makes the lesson stronger: God defeats the 'mighty' טיטוס with something this small and lacking.

keyTerms.meaning: An entrance (an opening for taking food in)
An exit (an opening for letting waste out)
It has / it does not have

phrases.english: Because it has an entrance,
but it does not have an exit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The gnat is lowly because it can take food in but has no way to let waste out.

steps.title: The gnat enters טיטוס's brain for seven years
steps.stepSummary: The בת קול tells טיטוס to go up on land and fight the gnat. He goes up, and a gnat enters his nose and picks at his brain for seven years.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Go up onto dry land and make war with it.' He went up onto dry land. A gnat came, entered his nostril, and picked at his brain for seven years.
steps.whatsHappening: Back to the story: the בת קול finishes its words, and the punishment begins as soon as טיטוס reaches land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: טיטוס wanted a fight on land, and he gets one, against a gnat. The 'mighty' conqueror who mocked God suffers for years from the weakest creature in the world.

phrases.english: Go up onto dry land
phrases.notes: The בת קול is still talking here. The story picks up right where it stopped before the question about the gnat.

phrases.english: and make war with it.
He went up onto dry land;
a gnat came and entered his nostril,
and picked at his brain for seven years.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the story after the side question about the gnat (steps 22 and 23).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A gnat enters טיטוס's nose and torments his brain for seven years.

steps.title: The blacksmith's hammer helps only for thirty days
steps.stepSummary: טיטוס finds that the sound of a blacksmith's hammer quiets the gnat. He hires blacksmiths to pound before him every day, but after thirty days the gnat gets used to the noise.
steps.simpleTranslation: One day he was passing by the door of a blacksmith's shop. The gnat heard the sound of the hammer and went quiet. He said: 'There is a remedy.' Every day they would bring a blacksmith who would hammer in front of him. To a non-Jew he gave four זוזים; to a Jew he said: 'It is enough for you that you see your enemy suffer.' He did this for thirty days. From then on, once the gnat got used to it, it got used to it.
steps.whatsHappening: The story shows טיטוס searching for relief. He finds one that works for a while, and then it stops working.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The remedy only works for a short time, which shows that טיטוס cannot escape his punishment. The detail about the Jewish blacksmith shows that even while suffering, טיטוס still treats the Jews with contempt, while their 'payment' is seeing their enemy in pain.

keyTerms.meaning: Once it got used to it, it got used to it

phrases.english: One day he was passing by
the door of a blacksmith's shop;
it heard the sound of the hammer and went quiet.
phrases.notes: It's the gnat that hears the hammer and goes still, not טיטוס.

phrases.english: He said: There is a remedy.
Every day they would bring a blacksmith
and they would hammer in front of him.
To a non-Jew he would give four זוזים;
to a Jew he would say:
It is enough for you that you see your enemy suffer.
phrases.notes: טיטוס means himself. Seeing him in pain is the Jew's only 'payment.'

phrases.english: For thirty days he did this;
from then on,
once it got used to it, it got used to it.
phrases.notes: Literally 'once it trampled, it trampled.' The gnat got used to the noise and went back to picking at his brain.

steps.triggerLanguage: יוֹמָא חַד הֲוָה קָא חָלֵיף אַבָּבָא דְּבֵי נַפָּחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the seven years of suffering from step 24 and tells of a failed attempt at a cure.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Hammering quieted the gnat for thirty days, but then it got used to the noise and the suffering came back.

steps.title: רבי פנחס בן ערובא sees the gnat after טיטוס dies
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי פנחס בן ערובא, who was among the great men of Rome. When טיטוס died, they opened his skull and found the gnat had grown as big as a sparrow, weighing two סלעים.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: רבי פנחס בן ערובא said: I was among the great men of Rome. When he died, they split open his skull and found inside something like a sparrow, weighing two סלעים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with an eyewitness account of how the story ended. It describes what was found in טיטוס's head.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This adds an eyewitness who was there when it happened. Over the years the tiny 'lowly' gnat grew into something the size of a bird, which shows how great the punishment had become.

keyTerms.meaning: It was taught in a ברייתא
סלעים, a coin also used as a weight

steps.whatToRemember: The 'lowly' gnat, the weakest creature, was enough to bring down the man who destroyed the בית המקדש and mocked God.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי פִּנְחָס בֶּן עֲרוּבָא:
phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Pinchas ben Aruva said:
I was among the great men of Rome,
and when he died they split open his skull,
phrases.notes: 'He' is טיטוס.

phrases.english: and found in it something like a sparrow
weighing two סלעים.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי פִּנְחָס בֶּן עֲרוּבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the gnat story with an eyewitness account of what was found after טיטוס died.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When טיטוס died, the gnat in his brain had grown to the size of a sparrow weighing two סלעים.

steps.title: Another ברייתא: like a year-old pigeon
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא gives a different description: the creature was like a one-year-old pigeon, weighing two ליטרין.
steps.simpleTranslation: In a ברייתא it was taught: like a one-year-old young pigeon, weighing two ליטרין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ברייתא that tells the same detail a bit differently, describing the creature's size and weight in other terms.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sources agree that the gnat grew into something bird-sized. They differ only in which bird they compare it to and how much it weighed: a pigeon at two ליטרין versus a sparrow at two סלעים.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא, a teaching from the time of the משנה

phrases.english: In a ברייתא it was taught:
like a one-year-old young pigeon,
weighing two ליטרין.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another version of the description in step 26.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Another version: the creature was like a one-year-old pigeon weighing two ליטרין.

steps.title: The creature had a copper mouth and iron claws
steps.stepSummary: אביי reports a tradition that the creature found in טיטוס's skull had a mouth of copper and claws of iron.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: We have a tradition that its mouth was made of copper and its claws were made of iron.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי adds one more detail about the creature that was found inside טיטוס's head.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two ברייתות before this described the creature's size and weight. אביי adds what it was made of, a copper mouth and iron claws. This shows how hard and painful the punishment was.

keyTerms.meaning: We have a tradition (literally: we hold)

phrases.english: Abaye said: We have a tradition,
its mouth was of copper
and its claws were of iron.
phrases.notes: "Its" is the gnat that grew inside טיטוס's head, from the steps just before.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a further detail to the ברייתות that described the creature found in טיטוס's skull.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The creature had a copper mouth and iron claws.

steps.title: טיטוס orders his ashes scattered to escape judgment
steps.stepSummary: As he is dying, טיטוס tells his servants to burn his body and scatter the ashes over the seven seas so that God cannot find him and judge him.
steps.simpleTranslation: When טיטוס was dying, he said to them: Burn that man (meaning me), and scatter his ashes over the seven seas, so that the God of the Jews will not find him and bring him to judgment.
steps.whatsHappening: טיטוס gives his last order before he dies. He tries to hide from God's judgment by having his ashes scattered everywhere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even after all his suffering, טיטוס still thinks he can escape God. He talks about himself as "that man" instead of saying "me." The next story shows that his plan did not work, because he is being judged after death.
steps.whatToRemember: טיטוס suffers in his life and then tries to run from God's judgment after death. The coming story shows he cannot escape it.

phrases.english: When he was dying,
he said to them: Burn that man
phrases.notes: "That man" is טיטוס talking about himself. He avoids saying "me" for something bad.

phrases.english: and scatter his ashes over the seven seas,
so that the God of the Jews will not find him
and stand him up for judgment.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הֲוָה קָא מָיֵית, אֲמַר לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the story of טיטוס's life with his death and his last order.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: טיטוס ordered his body burned and his ashes scattered to avoid God's judgment.

steps.title: אונקלוס raises טיטוס and asks who is most important
steps.stepSummary: אונקלוס, the son of טיטוס's sister, wants to convert. He raises טיטוס from the dead and asks him who is most important in the next world.
steps.simpleTranslation: אונקלוס bar קלוניקוס was the son of טיטוס's sister. He wanted to convert. He went and raised טיטוס from the dead by sorcery and asked him: Who is important in that world?
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. אונקלוס is thinking about converting, so he calls up טיטוס from the dead and asks him a question. This sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: טיטוס tried to escape judgment, but now he is reached after death. אונקלוס wants honest information from someone who can see the next world before he decides whether to join the Jews.

keyTerms.meaning: Onkelos, the nephew of טיטוס who later became a famous convert
Sorcery used to raise the dead
That world, meaning the next world where the dead are

phrases.english: Onkelos bar Kalonikos
was the son of Titus's sister.
He wanted to convert.
He went and raised Titus through sorcery,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאן חֲשִׁיב בְּהָהוּא עָלְמָא?
phrases.english: and said to him: Who is important in that world?

steps.triggerLanguage: אוּנְקְלוֹס בַּר קְלוֹנִיקוּס בַּר אֲחָתֵיהּ דְּטִיטוּס הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story that continues the theme of טיטוס's fate after death.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who has the most importance in the next world.

steps.title: טיטוס answers: the Jewish people
steps.stepSummary: טיטוס admits that ישראל are the most important in the next world.
steps.simpleTranslation: טיטוס said to him: The Jewish people.
steps.whatsHappening: טיטוס answers the first question. He says ישראל are the most important.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The enemy who destroyed the בית המקדש now has to admit that the Jewish people are the most important. This sets up אונקלוס's next question.

phrases.english: He said to him: The Jewish people.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אונקלוס's question from step 30.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: ישראל are the most important in the next world.

steps.title: Should I join them?
steps.stepSummary: אונקלוס asks טיטוס whether he should attach himself to the Jewish people.
steps.simpleTranslation: אונקלוס asked: Should I attach myself to them?
steps.whatsHappening: Since ישראל are the most important, אונקלוס asks the natural next question: should he join them? This sets up טיטוס's advice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the real question behind the whole visit, because אונקלוס wants to convert. He is checking whether it is worth it.

phrases.english: What about attaching myself to them?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on טיטוס's answer that ישראל are the most important.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether אונקלוס should join the Jewish people.

steps.title: טיטוס advises fighting ישראל instead
steps.stepSummary: טיטוס says the Jews have too many commandments to keep. He advises אונקלוס to attack them instead and become a leader, and he quotes a פסוק from איכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: טיטוס said to him: Their commandments are many, and you will not be able to keep them. Go and attack them in that world, and you will become a head, as it is written: "Her adversaries have become the head". Anyone who causes distress to ישראל becomes a head.
steps.whatsHappening: טיטוס tries to talk אונקלוס out of converting. He tells him to fight the Jews instead and backs this up with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: טיטוס admits ישראל are the most important, but he still pushes אונקלוס against them. He reads the word צריה (her enemies) in the פסוק to mean that anyone who causes trouble (מיצר) for ישראל ends up on top. His advice still comes from his hatred of the Jews.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not take טיטוס's advice as the גמרא's own lesson. He is a wicked man speaking. The story shows that even he must admit ישראל are the most important.

phrases.english: He said to him: Their commandments are many,
and you will not be able to keep them.
Go, attack them in that world
phrases.notes: Speaking from among the dead, טיטוס means the world of the living, where אונקלוס is.

phrases.english: and you will become a head,
as it is written: "Her adversaries have become the head, etc."
phrases.notes: איכה 1:5

phrases.english: Anyone who causes distress to Israel becomes a head.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אונקלוס's question about joining the Jews.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Do not join them, because the commandments are too many. Fight them instead and become a leader, based on איכה 1:5.

steps.title: What is טיטוס's own punishment?
steps.stepSummary: אונקלוס asks טיטוס what punishment "that man" (טיטוס himself) receives, and טיטוס begins to answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: אונקלוס said to him: What is the punishment of that man? טיטוס said to him:
steps.whatsHappening: אונקלוס asks about טיטוס's own punishment in the next world. The answer starts here and continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This question checks whether טיטוס's plan to escape judgment worked. The answer will show what happens to someone who causes distress to ישראל, which tests his own advice.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דִּינֵיהּ דְּהָהוּא גַּבְרָא בְּמַאי?
phrases.english: He said to him: What is the punishment of that man?
phrases.notes: "That man" is a polite way of saying טיטוס himself, so אונקלוס does not say "your punishment" outright.

phrases.english: He said to him:
phrases.notes: טיטוס's answer continues on the next amud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דִּינֵיהּ דְּהָהוּא גַּבְרָא בְּמַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After hearing טיטוס's advice, אונקלוס asks about טיטוס's own fate.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What punishment טיטוס receives in the next world.
